title: DMZ mine blast
ticker: BREAKING: Probe concludes North Korea planted the DMZ mines that wounded 3 South Korean soldiers
One officer lost a foot in the Sept. 21 blast
Seoul raises the case at the U.N., demands an apology from Pyongyang
North Korea denies involvement, Kim Yo Jong mocks Seoul
Unification Minister under fire for calling it "a regrettable accident"

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to KOWEN News.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Tonight, rising tension on the Korean Peninsula. Investigators have concluded that the landmines that wounded three South Korean soldiers inside the DMZ were *planted by North Korea*.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: One officer *lost a foot*. Pyongyang denies everything. And in Seoul, the government's own response has become a political fight.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: It is the most serious mine incident on the border in over a decade.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Now the dispute has reached the *United Nations*. Here's what happened.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: It happened on September twenty first, inside the *Demilitarized Zone*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Officers from a frontline unit of the Army's *25th Infantry Division* were carrying out a search operation near the boundary of Paju and Yeoncheon, north of Seoul.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Then, a landmine *exploded*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Three officers were wounded. Two were seriously hurt, including a reconnaissance battalion commander, whose *foot was severed*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: It was the first time in *eleven years* that a mine blast south of the border line had caused serious injuries in the DMZ.

facts: ~2 million mines in and around it

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The DMZ runs *two hundred forty eight kilometers* across the Korean Peninsula, and about four kilometers wide.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: An estimated *two million mines* lie in and around it.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice, not a peace treaty, so the two Koreas are *technically still at war*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: And since 2024, when Kim Jong Un declared the South North Korea's *principal enemy*, Pyongyang has been laying new mines and building barriers along the border.

scenes.name: Lt. Gen. Kwon Dae-won
scenes.role: Vice Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff
scenes.quote: We assess that North Korean landmines are highly suspected to have caused the blast.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: A week later, South Korea's military gave its first assessment.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Based on the crater, the pattern of the flames and the soldiers' injuries, Lieutenant General Kwon Dae-won said North Korean landmines were *highly suspected*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The blast site was only about *ten meters* from an area where North Korean troops were believed to have recently planted mines.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He warned that if Pyongyang was responsible, the military would take *appropriate and corresponding measures*.

items.text: Probe: mines planted by N. Korea

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: On October fifth, the joint investigation by South Korea's military and the *U.N. Command* reached its conclusion.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The two mines that exploded had been *planted by North Korea*. Forensic tests identified a North Korean made plastic anti-personnel mine.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: A *third mine*, which had not exploded, was also found near the site, and troops removed the remaining North Korean mines.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: South Korea's defense ministry concluded the mine laying *violated the Armistice Agreement*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: For many South Koreans, the blast brought back memories of *2015*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: That August, North Korean soldiers crossed more than four hundred forty meters south of the border line and buried *wooden box mines* near a South Korean guard post.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Staff Sergeant Ha Jae-hun lost *both legs*, and Staff Sergeant Kim Jung-won lost his right leg.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: But this time, much of the anger in South Korea has been aimed at *its own government*.

scenes.name: Lee Jae-myung
scenes.quote: The military authorities must transparently establish the facts of the case through a swift and thorough investigation.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: President Lee Jae-myung first addressed the blast in public *eight days* after it happened, at a Cabinet meeting.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He called for a swift and thorough investigation, in close cooperation with the U.N. Command.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But critics seized on his description of the blast as an *unexpected accident*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The controversy exploded on October seventh, during a parliamentary audit of the Unification Ministry.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Unification Minister Chung Dong-young called the blast *a regrettable accident*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He said the most essential task was ending the long war on the Korean Peninsula and building a *peace regime*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He also said it was *not yet possible* to confirm the blast as an attack.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Independent lawmaker Han Dong-hoon fired back. How can burying mines on our side of the line be an *unexpected accident*?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He said no one was holding North Korea *accountable* for planting mines that injured South Korean troops.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Chung replied that *hostility and hatred* created this situation, and that resolving them is the fundamental answer.

scenes.name: Kim Yo Jong
scenes.role: Kim Jong Un's sister · Workers' Party official
scenes.quote: A spectacle too good to watch alone.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Pyongyang was watching. On October eighth, Kim Jong Un's sister, *Kim Yo Jong*, issued a statement through state media mocking Seoul.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: She called the debate in South Korea *a spectacle too good to watch alone*, and an endless dogfight over whether it was an accident or a provocation.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: She also seized on Minister Chung's words, claiming a South Korean official had *confessed* it was hard to call the blast a deliberate attack.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: She also took offense at Seoul's request for a U.N. sanctions exemption to send *medical equipment* to the North, treating it as an insult.

scenes.name: Cha Ji-hoon
scenes.role: South Korea's Ambassador to the U.N.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The same day, Seoul took the case to the *United Nations*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Ambassador Cha Ji-hoon told a U.N. General Assembly committee that the blast was caused by a mine *deliberately buried* south of the border by North Korean troops.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He called it *a clear violation* of the Armistice Agreement.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: North Korea, he said, must halt escalatory actions, *offer an apology*, and take responsible steps.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun has said Seoul's options include seeking a *Security Council* resolution or statement.

scenes.name: North Korean delegate
scenes.role: Right of reply · U.N. General Assembly

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: North Korea's delegation took the unusual step of demanding a *right of reply*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Its representative called the accusation *a poor trick* by the South Korean military to shift its own responsibility onto North Korea.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: And he declared that the North would defend its territory through *strength, not negotiations*.

scenes.name: Kim Jong Un
scenes.quote: 5 statements denying the blast, all to foreign audiences. Not a word to North Koreans at home.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Back in Pyongyang, there is a notable *silence*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: North Korea has issued *five statements* denying responsibility, but all through outward facing media. Its own people have not been told about the blast.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Kim Jong Un appeared on Saturday at an event marking the Workers' Party anniversary, with his wife and daughter, but made *no comment*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: That is a sharp contrast with *2015*, when North Korea broadcast its denials on state television, aimed squarely at its own citizens.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Analysts say Pyongyang may not want tensions to *delay* its border fortification work.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification said the North seems intent on *avoiding construction delays* on its border project.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The mine dispute is playing out against a bigger diplomatic chill.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: At the U.N. General Assembly last month, North Korean diplomats sat through President Trump's speech, but *left their seats* during President Lee's address.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: North Korea's vice foreign minister, Kim Son-gyong, told the assembly that its status as a *nuclear weapons state* cannot be reversed under any circumstances.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He also criticized Washington for backing South Korea's push for *nuclear powered submarines*.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Meanwhile, President Trump is still seeking *direct talks* with Kim Jong Un, while Seoul is pushing for a bigger role in peninsula affairs.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: To recap tonight's top story.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: A joint investigation has concluded that North Korea *planted the mines* that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ last month.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Seoul is now demanding an *apology* at the United Nations, while Pyongyang denies any role.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: At home, President Lee's government faces criticism for calling it an *accident*.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: With North and South refusing to talk face to face, the risk of the next incident remains *very real*.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: We'll keep following this story. That's all for tonight. This has been KOWEN News. Thanks for watching, and good night.
